young.html: Epictetus (say it ep-ick-TEE-tus) was born a slave, about 1,950 years ago. He walked with a limp. But he grew up to be one of the most famous teachers in the Roman world, and an emperor read his lessons.

His big idea was simple. Some things are up to us, and some things are not. What we think, what we choose and how we act are up to us. The weather, other people’s opinions and whether we win are not. Epictetus said that if we put our worry and effort into the things that are up to us, and accept the rest calmly, we can be free and steady inside, even when things go wrong.

young.name: gb-up-to-us
young.cap: Sort each card. Is it up to you or not? Then press Check.

young.html: The two-column worry list. Fold a paper in half. On the left write “Up to me,” on the right “Not up to me.” Write down three things that are bothering you this week, each in the right column. For each one on the left, write one small thing you can do. For each one on the right, write a sentence about how you could face it calmly. Talk it over with a grown-up.
Epictetus used the word Zeus, or God, often, and taught that the world is guided by a wise providence. That was part of his Stoic faith.

full.html: Epictetus was born around AD 50 at Hierapolis in Phrygia (in today’s Turkey) and was a slave in Rome in the household of Epaphroditus, a powerful freedman of the emperor Nero. He was lame; one story blamed a cruel master, but an ancient commentator says he was weak and lame from early on. His master let him study with the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus. Freed, he taught philosophy in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers from the city, around AD 93. He then opened a school at Nicopolis in western Greece, where students came from all over the empire, and he died there around AD 135.

Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. A student, Arrian of Nicomedia (later a governor and historian), took down his talks. Four books of these Discourses survive out of eight, and Arrian also made a short summary, the Encheiridion or Handbook, which means something you keep “in hand.”

full.text: Up to us, and not up to us

full.html: The Handbook opens with Epictetus’s central idea.

full.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion (turning from a thing); and in a word, whatever are our own acts: not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance: but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others.
full.author: Epictetus
full.note: Long’s Greek words in brackets are left out.

full.html: The Greek phrase is eph’ hēmin, “up to us.” What is up to us is our prohairesis, our power of choice: how we judge things, what we want and avoid, what we decide to do. Everything else, even our own bodies, depends at least partly on things outside us.

full.name: gb-up-to-us
full.cap: Eight cards. Sort them by Epictetus’s rule, then check.

full.text: It is our opinions that disturb us

Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things: for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were, it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death, that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
full.author: Epictetus

full.html: Epictetus does not say that bad things are not bad, or that people should not try to change the world. He says that our distress comes from the judgment we add to events, and that the judgment is ours to examine. A student who fails a test feels the failure; what turns it into “I am worthless” is an opinion, and opinions can be tested.
In the first of the Discourses, Epictetus imagines a man threatened by a tyrant, and shows what such a man should keep ready in his mind.

full.text: What is mine, and what is not mine; and what is permitted to me, and what is not permitted to me. I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament? I must go into exile. Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment?
full.author: Epictetus

full.html: Epictetus’s teaching can be set out as a simple argument. The premises are his; whether they are true is the real question.

head: Statement
rows: Only what is up to us can be truly good or bad for us.
Other people’s opinions of us are not up to us.
So other people’s opinions of us are not truly good or bad for us.
full.cap: The form is valid: if both premises are true, the conclusion must be. Critics question Premise 1.

full.html: Thinking Stoics try to feel nothing. Epictetus wants his students to love their families, keep their duties and act justly. What he tries to remove are the disturbing passions that come from false judgments, such as treating money or praise as if they were the most important things in life. His goal is calm, steady action, not coldness.

items: Marcus Aurelius, the next rung, thanks his teacher Rusticus for lending him the notes of Epictetus’s lectures.
Later readers, Christian and not, used the Handbook as a guide to self-discipline for centuries; it was adapted for monks in the Middle Ages.
Modern psychology: the founders of cognitive therapy, Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, named Epictetus’s saying about opinions as one source of their idea that how we interpret events shapes how we feel.

deep.html: Stoicism began in Athens around 300 BC with Zeno of Citium, who taught in a painted porch, the stoa, which gave the school its name. By Epictetus’s day it was the leading philosophy among educated Romans; Seneca, Nero’s adviser, was a Stoic too. Epictetus taught it as a way of life rather than as a set of theories: daily practice, self-examination and training in how to respond to events. He also taught that all people share in reason and are akin to God, so that a slave and an emperor are equally capable of freedom.

items: Is anything outside our control truly good or bad for us? What about health, friends or justice?
If we accept what we cannot change, will we stop trying to change things that are wrong?
Can a person in chains be free? What kind of freedom would that be?
Is Epictetus’s idea comforting, demanding, or both?

deep.html: Marcus Aurelius turned these lessons into an emperor’s private notebook. Augustine, later in this era, honored the Stoics’ seriousness but held that true peace comes from God’s grace, not from the will alone. Pascal, in the 17th century, praised Epictetus for seeing human greatness and blamed him for not seeing human weakness. Montaigne drew on the Stoics in his essays on how to face pain and death.

questions: Name something that went wrong this week. What part of it was up to you, and what part was not?
Epictetus says it is our opinion about a thing that disturbs us. Can you think of a time when changing how you thought about something changed how you felt?
Is what other people think of you up to you? Should you care about it at all?
Epictetus was a slave who taught that he was free inside. What do you think he meant?
If you accept the things you cannot change, how do you decide which things those are?
